verses.translation_literal: And Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that [was] his, and Lot with him, to the Negev.
verses.translation_dramatic: So Abram came up out of Egypt, climbing out of the black river-land into the hard bright country of the south, and with him, the whole caravan: his wife beside him, everything he owned, and Lot, never more than a step behind. Before them lay the Negev, dry and wide.
verses.directors_commentary:
Egypt is a descent in the Bible's geography even though it lies south of Canaan on the map: you 'go down' to the Nile and 'go up' to the hill country, and the verb here (wayya'al) marks the return. The famine that drove Abram there (12:10) is over, and so is the shame of the episode with Pharaoh; the stress falls on the little phrase 'he and his wife and all that was his', which quietly says that nothing was lost, not even Sarai, whom the text no longer names. Ramban and Radak both read this as a mark of the miracle: Pharaoh's gifts were not clawed back. Note that the pointed pronoun 'he' (hu') is redundant in Hebrew; it is there for emphasis, the survivor naming himself at the border.

The KJV 'into the south' hides that Negev is a proper name for a region, a semi-arid band of grazing land south of Hebron and Beersheba, where flocks live on winter rain. For an audience of herders this is the first stop on the road home, the territory where a big household can move without trespassing on farm land.

philological_notes.note: The final -ah is the directional he, 'toward the Negev'. Negev is a proper noun but also the common word for 'south' in Hebrew, because the region lay south of the central hills. Rashi on Genesis 13:1 takes it as the southern part of the land.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram [was] very heavy in livestock, in silver and in gold.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abram was a heavy man now, heavy with wealth: herds that darkened the hillsides, silver in weighed pieces, and gold besides.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew adjective kaved means 'heavy', and 'honour' and 'wealth' come from the same root (kavod): in the ancient world a rich man literally weighs more. Ibn Ezra stresses this and Rashi glosses the word as 'laden with burdens', which is why the caravan moves slowly in the next verse. The KJV 'rich' is fair but flattens the image.

The order is the order of an economy before coinage: livestock first, because flocks are the capital, then silver and gold, which were weighed out, not counted. The wealth is the legacy of Egypt (12:16), a detail the text lets the reader remember rather than repeat.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'heavy'; the same root gives kavod, 'glory/honour'. Ibn Ezra connects it with 'heavy as a stone' (Prov 27:3), the opposite of qalon, 'lightness/shame'.

verses.translation_literal: And he went on his journeyings from the Negev and as far as Bethel, as far as the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and the Ai,
verses.translation_dramatic: So he went on, stage by slow stage, up out of the Negev, the dry south, his herds setting the pace. On he went to Bethel, and past it to the very place where his tent had first stood, between Bethel and the Ai.
verses.directors_commentary:
The plural 'journeyings' (massa'av) is the word for pulling up tent pegs and moving camp; Abram does not walk, he migrates, and the verse is written at the speed of a flock. Radak reads it as 'stage after short stage', because Abram was very heavy in livestock (v. 2): a rich man travels slowly. Rashi, drawing on Genesis Rabbah, adds a lesson in manners: on the way back from Egypt he lodged at the same inns where he had lodged going down, since a man should not change his lodgings. Ibn Ezra hears a pilgrimage: he comes to the altar to give thanks that he arrived in peace.

The Negev is not 'the south' as a compass point but a named region of dry steppe south of the hill country, the first place he settled and the place famine drove him out of (12:9–10). The KJV 'from the south' is acceptable, but it hides that this is the same country-name as in Genesis 12. 'At the beginning' (battechillah) points back to 12:8, where he pitched his tent here and built an altar. The text sends him back to the exact spot of his first worship, between two towns, one of which is called 'the Ai' (ha-'Ay), literally 'the ruin' with the definite article; the KJV 'Hai' is a transliteration of the article-plus-name, not a different place.

philological_notes.note: 'His journeyings': from the verb for pulling up tent pegs to break camp. The plural describes a migration made in stages, not one march.
'At the beginning': ties this arrival back to Abram's first camp and altar at 12:8.
Written אָהֳלֹה (with final he), read 'his tent'. The Ketiv/Qere difference does not change the sense.

verses.translation_literal: To the place of the altar which he had made there at the first, and Abram called there in the name of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: He came to the place of the altar, the altar he had built there long ago, and there, once more, Abram called out in the name of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a homecoming liturgy. The altar of Genesis 12:8 is still standing, a pile of fieldstones in a land of strangers, and Abram's first act is not to unload the camels but to call. Radak notes that a man should fix a place for his prayer, because the heart is steadier in a familiar spot, and he reads 'there' as a second calling, not just a recollection of the first (so also Rashi's alternative). Onkelos renders the verb 'prayed'.

The KJV 'called upon the name' is acceptable, but the Hebrew idiom qara' be-shem is closer to 'proclaim in the name of', a public declaration and not only a private plea. The Egyptian detour is over; the one who was silent before Pharaoh now speaks aloud again.

philological_notes.note: 'Called in the name of YHWH': to proclaim or invoke the name, not necessarily to pray privately. Onkelos translates it as 'prayed'. Rashi suggests it could mean he called now, afresh, or refer back to the earlier calling.

verses.translation_literal: And also to Lot, the one going with Abram, there were sheep and cattle and tents.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Lot too, who had walked at Abram's side all this way, had flocks of his own, and herds, and tents.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'also' (gam) is the whole drama in one word. Radak: it adds to the previous verse, so Lot's riches are set beside Abram's, and the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Radak both say that they came 'through the merit of Abram'. Rashi puts it sharply: who made this possible? His going with Abram.

The participle 'going with' is the tell: Lot is a follower, but the following has made him a chieftain. 'Tents' (ohalim), unusual in this list, means many households, hired hands and dependants (Radak): Lot is not a nephew with a donkey but the head of a camp. The KJV 'herds' for baqar is fine; 'flocks' for tson is sheep and goats together.

philological_notes.note: Plural of ohel, 'tent'. Radak takes it as a sign of many households and dependants; Ibn Ezra discusses its unusual vocalization.

verses.translation_literal: And not did the land bear them to dwell together, for their substance was much, and they were not able to dwell together.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the land could not carry them. Not the two of them together. Their wealth was too great, too heavy, and the hills that had held one household would not hold two. They could not dwell side by side.
verses.directors_commentary:
The land 'bears' (nasa') them as a back bears a load, and the verb is masculine although 'land' is feminine, a quirk Radak notes by comparing Isaiah 9:18. Rashi supplies what the verse leaves unsaid: the land could not carry enough pasture for their herds. Radak is more concrete: grazing was tight, because Canaanite shepherds were already using the same hills, and the herdsmen of each side pressed on the other. The KJV 'the land was not able to bear them' is faithful; the BBE 'not wide enough' loses the image of weight.

The verse says the same thing twice, 'could not dwell together' (lashevet yachdav), once about the land and once about the men. The repetition is the drumbeat of the scene: it is the verse's whole argument. In a society with no fodder markets, wealth meant animals and animals meant grass; two large herds on one range was a collision waiting to happen. The 'substance' (rekhush) is the movable property of a clan: livestock, silver, servants, tents.

philological_notes.note: 'Their substance, acquired goods': movable property gathered by a household. The word recurs in 12:5 (what Abram gathered before leaving Haran), in 14:11–12 (the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot's goods taken with him), in 14:16 (the goods Abram brings back), and in 15:14 (the great substance Abram's seed will take from the land of bondage). It is the word for wealth that can be carried off.
'Bear, lift': the land as a carrier of a load. The same verb opens verse 10, where Lot 'lifts' his eyes.
'Together': occurs twice in this verse; Ibn Ezra notes it as a rare, archaic form.

verses.translation_literal: And there was strife between the herdsmen of the livestock of Abram and between the herdsmen of the livestock of Lot, and the Canaanite and the Perizzite [were] then dwelling in the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the quarrel came, first between the herdsmen, rough men shouting across a shrinking well and a trampled pasture, Abram's men against Lot's. And all the while the Canaanite and the Perizzite looked on, for they were living in the land then.
verses.directors_commentary:
The word 'strife' (riv) is a legal-flavored term: it is a quarrel that could end in a lawsuit or a fight. It begins with the hired men, not the masters; Abram will step in at once to stop it in verse 8. Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah, adds a midrash that Lot's herdsmen let their animals graze in other people's fields and justified themselves by saying the land was promised to Abram and Lot was his heir. This is midrash, not what the text says, and Ramban objects that the promise was to Abram's seed, not to Lot.

The last clause is a warning: the land is not empty. Sforno says the quarrel between two resident aliens made them look like men of strife in the eyes of the locals, and Ramban says Abram feared they might be driven out by force. The KJV 'cattle' for miqneh is too narrow; the word covers sheep, goats, donkeys and camels, all livestock.

philological_notes.note: Strife, quarrel, with the sense of a legal dispute. The related form meriva appears in verse 8.
'Then, at that time'. Ramban reads it as a hint that the peoples in the land were semi-nomadic at this period and moved their grazing grounds from year to year.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram said to Lot, "Let there not, please, be strife between me and between you, and between my herdsmen and between your herdsmen, for we [are] men, brothers."
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Abram spoke to Lot, gently, as one speaks to family. "Let there be no quarrel between you and me, I beg you, nor between my herdsmen and yours. We are brothers."
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram, the elder and the senior partner, opens with 'please' (na'), a particle of courtesy he does not owe a nephew. He moves the issue from the herdsmen up to the masters ('between me and you'), then back down, and Radak notes why: if the herdsmen fight, the masters cannot stay clear of it. The nephew is called a 'brother', as Hebrew often does for close kin; Rashi adds a midrash that the two men looked alike.

The phrase 'men, brothers' (anashim achim) is odd; YLT's 'men--brethren' keeps its rhythm. It means 'men who are kin', an emphasis that the KJV 'we be brethren' rounds off.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'men, brothers', a kin pair; Rashi explains it as 'relatives', with an aggadic reading that they looked alike.

verses.translation_literal: Is not all the land before you? Separate yourself, please, from upon me. If the left, then I will go right; and if the right, then I will go left.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look: the whole land lies open before you. Part from me, I ask. If you take the left hand, I will go to the right; if you take the right, I will go to the left. The choice is yours.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is one of the great acts of generosity in the Bible. Abram, who holds the promise of the land (12:7), gives the first choice to the younger man. Radak: 'my soul is wide, and for my brother I give the choice'. The Hebrew is gracious but firm, because 'separate yourself' is an imperative, however much 'please' softens it.

The verbs for left and right (ve'eimina, ve'asme'ila) are made from the nouns, 'let me right-hand it' and 'let me left-hand it'. The KJV smooths this into 'go to the right'. In the Near East one faced east to orient: left was north, right was south, and the targums translate it that way. Abram's offer is therefore a choice between the hill country to the north and the Negev to the south, and he does not foresee that Lot will take neither (verse 11).

philological_notes.note: A denominative verb from yamin, 'right', in the cohortative: 'let me take the right'. Rashi compares the parallel ve'asme'ila, 'let me take the left', and the form in 2 Sam 14:19.
'Separate yourself from upon me'. The root pr-d is the same that will appear in verse 11 when the two men actually part; Radak notes that it is Lot who goes, in fulfilment of Abram's word.

verses.translation_literal: And Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the disc of the Jordan, that all of it [was] well-watered, before YHWH destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of YHWH, like the land of Egypt, as you come [to] Zoar.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Lot lifted up his eyes. Far below him, the whole round plain of the Jordan lay green and shining, watered everywhere, as lush as the garden of the LORD, as fertile as the fields of Egypt, all the way to Zoar. This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Lifted up his eyes and saw' is the biblical phrase for a decisive look, here the opposite of Abram's act in verse 4: Abram called on the Name, Lot looks and desires. The narrator's aside, 'before YHWH destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah', is the shadow over the picture, a warning to the audience before Lot knows. Rashi's tradition (Genesis Rabbah) adds that choosing to live among such people was itself a judgment on him; the text does not say so.

The double simile joins Eden ('the garden of YHWH', Gen 2:10) with Egypt, and Ramban (citing Deut 11:10) points out the common thread: both are watered by a river, not by rain. The audience knows Egypt as the land where Abram and Lot have just been, so the image is of a place of plenty that is also a place of danger. The KJV rendering 'the plain' for kikkar hides the image: a kikkar is a 'disc', a round loaf, the circular basin of the Jordan.

philological_notes.note: Kikkar means 'round disc' and so 'circle, round plain'; it is also the word for a round loaf and a talent of metal. Targum Onkelos renders it 'plain' (meishar), as does Rashi.
Two images of a well-watered land: Eden and Egypt. Ramban links the two with irrigated land (Deut 11:10), while the rabbis (Sifre) assign 'garden of YHWH' to trees and 'land of Egypt' to crops.

verses.translation_literal: And Lot chose for himself all the Plain of the Jordan, and Lot set out from the east, and they separated, a man from upon his brother.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Lot chose. For himself, the text says: for himself, the whole Plain of the Jordan. Then Lot struck his tents and set out from the east, and the two men parted, each from beside his brother.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the dative: 'chose for himself' (bachar lo) is a man looking after himself. Abram had offered the first choice and Lot takes all of it ('all the Plain', kol-kikkar), not a share, and the verb 'set out' (vayyissa') is the tent-peg verb of verse 3. The KJV's 'chose him' is archaic English for the same dative, and its 'journeyed east' commits to one reading of a disputed word.

Miqqedem is literally 'from the east', or 'from aforetime'. Rashi takes it as 'from the east': Lot journeyed away from Abram, to Abram's west, so he travelled from east to west. Ibn Ezra and Sforno agree on the direction (Sforno stresses that Lot took neither the 'right' nor the 'left' he had been offered). Radak takes the opposite view, moving toward the east, and reads the mem as the one in 'from the Negev' in verse 3. Rashi also gives a midrash on the same word: Lot 'removed himself from the Ancient One of the world', saying he wanted neither Abram nor his God.

The verse ends with the word 'brother' again, now in the past tense: 'a man from upon his brother', echoing Abram's plea 'we are brothers' (v. 8). The parting that Abram proposed is carried out, and the family tie is the last word.

philological_notes.note: 'From the east' or 'from aforetime'. Rashi: Lot moved away to Abram's west, so travelled from east to west; his midrash reads it as 'from the Ancient One of the world'. Radak reads it as eastward movement.
'He chose for himself': the reflexive dative marks self-interest; Lot selects the whole Plain, not a portion.
'A man from upon his brother': 'brother' returns from verse 8. Radak notes the oddity that both are said to part, though Lot was the one who left.

verses.translation_literal: Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelt in the cities of the disc, and pitched his tent as far as Sodom.
verses.translation_dramatic: Abram stayed in the land of Canaan. But Lot settled among the cities of the plain, and little by little his tent moved down the valley until it stood at Sodom.
verses.directors_commentary:
The balanced halves, 'Abram dwelt ... Lot dwelt', are the scales of the story. Abram stays within the promised land; Lot is in the 'cities' of the plain, not in the open grass, and the verb that closes the verse, 'and he pitched his tent' (wayye'ehal, from ohel), pulls the camp in step by step. Ramban reads the plural 'cities' as a tent shifting from place to place; Radak, that he moved from site to site until he reached Sodom. The Hebrew says 'as far as Sodom', the KJV 'toward' softens the destination.

For an ancient audience the sequence is the warning: a tent at the edge of a city is the first step to a house inside. The narrator will name Sodom's sin in the very next verse (13:13), but the geography here already says it.

philological_notes.note: A verb made from the noun ohel, 'tent': 'he tented', i.e. pitched or moved his tent. Rashi and Ibn Ezra gloss it as 'pitched tents'; Radak as moving from place to place.
'As far as Sodom': a limit, where the KJV has 'toward'. Ramban contrasts Lot's fixed settlement in one place with Abram's wandering throughout Canaan.

verses.translation_literal: And the men of Sodom [were] evil and sinners against YHWH exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the men of Sodom — and here the story lowers its voice — were wicked, and were sinners against the LORD, past all measure.
verses.directors_commentary: A narrator's aside, dropped like a stone into the quiet of the previous verse: while Lot's tent drifts toward Sodom, we are told what the reader knows and Lot does not. Play it as dramatic irony; the actors on stage do not hear it. The pairing is deliberate: 'evil' (ra'im) is wrong done to people, 'sinners' (chata'im) is a missing of the mark against God, and 'exceedingly' (me'od) closes the line with no softening. Rashi hears the first as bodily and the second as financial, and Radak reads both as the breaking of the commandments given to Adam and Noah; whatever the exact crimes, the narrator says the offence is against YHWH, not only against neighbours. The KJV's 'before the Lord' is gentler than it sounds: the Hebrew lamed can mean 'toward' or 'against', and the ASV 'against' is nearer the sense. Note also the word order: the KJV 'exceedingly' trails at the end exactly as in the Hebrew, a rare case where the old version keeps the punch. Sodom's fame as a city of the fertile plain (13:10) makes the judgment sharper: the best-watered land holds the worst people.

philological_notes.note: 'Sinners', an adjective-noun form from the root meaning to miss the mark. Here it is set against YHWH, so the fault is religious as well as social. Rashi takes 'sinners' to concern their money and 'evil' their bodies; Ibn Ezra takes 'evil' as towards people, citing Ezekiel 16:49.
A bare lamed: 'to', 'toward', or 'against' YHWH. Rashi reads it as conscious rebellion: they knew their Master and meant to defy him.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH said to Abram, after Lot separated from with him, "Lift up, please, your eyes and see, from the place where you [are] there: northward and southward and eastward and westward."
verses.translation_dramatic: And when Lot had gone — when the last of his herds had wound away down the slope and the hills were quiet again — the LORD spoke to Abram. "Lift up your eyes," he said. "Look, from the very place where you stand: to the north, to the south, to the east, to the west."
verses.directors_commentary: The timing is the whole point: 'after Lot separated from with him'. The voice that had been silent since the quarrel speaks only once the rival claimant is gone. Rashi says the word of God stays away from a man while a wicked one is beside him; Sforno reads it differently, that had it been said while Lot was present, Lot and his herdsmen might have pushed themselves forward to seize some of it. Either way, the actors should feel a release, as if the air had cleared. The command is physical: 'lift up your eyes' is the same gesture Lot made in 13:10, when he looked at the well-watered plain and chose. Abram, who chose nothing, is now told to look, and what he is given is wider than Lot's view. The four directions, each with a directional -ah ending (tzafonah, negbah, qedmah, yamah), are a surveyor's sweep from a hilltop near Bethel; 'yam' (sea) is the word for west because the Mediterranean lay that way, and 'negev' (dry south) names the region itself. The KJV 'northward' keeps the -ah ending well, but 'after that Lot was separated' is stiff: the Hebrew is a plain infinitive, 'after Lot's parting'. The KJV also omits the small particle na ('please'), softened to 'now', a courtesy that the Hebrew gives even to a divine command.

philological_notes.note: 'Lift up your eyes' echoes Lot's looking in 13:10, but here it is God who tells Abram where to look. The particle נָא softens the imperative into an invitation.

Four directions with the directional ending -ah: 'northward, southward, eastward, seaward'. Radak notes that north and south are named first because of what Abram had said to Lot about left and right; Lot's share is placed elsewhere.

verses.translation_literal: For all the land that you [are] seeing, to you I will give it, and to your seed, until forever.
verses.translation_dramatic: For all the land your eyes can hold — all of it — I will give to you, and to your children after you, for ever.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the legal heart of the speech, and the actors should hear the cadence of a grant. 'To you' comes before the verb, so the first thing Abram hears is that the land is his; 'and to your seed' follows, as a deed names heirs. The grant is built on sight: 'all the land that you are seeing'. Radak points out that Abram could not literally see it all, but that seeing a part stands for the whole, as when Moses is told 'see the land' (Deuteronomy 32:49). The land is given now, in the promise, even though others live in it: Radak says it is Abram's although it is in the hands of the nations, and his sons will drive them out. The Hebrew 'ad olam' is not a mathematical eternity but 'to the horizon of time'; Radak adds that even if the seed is exiled they will come back. The KJV 'for ever' is a fair match, and its 'will I give it' keeps the inverted order well. Ibn Ezra notes that 'I will give' here is by speech, a word that makes it so, as with the sin-offering goat in Leviticus 16:21.

philological_notes.note: 'I will give it', imperfect with a nun-energic suffix that adds emphasis. Ibn Ezra explains that giving here is by speech: God's word is itself the gift.
'Until perpetuity'. The word olam means a remote or hidden time; 'for ever' is its usual rendering. Radak reads it to mean that even after exile the seed will return.

verses.translation_literal: And I will set your seed like the dust of the earth, which, if a man is able to count the dust of the earth, also your seed will be counted.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will make your children like the dust of the earth — as many as the grains under your feet. Let a man try to count that dust, and then, only then, might your children be counted too.
verses.directors_commentary: The promise now moves from space to people, and from sight to the ground under Abram's sandals. Dust is the image of a dry country: it lies on every road, rises behind every herd, and nobody ever counts it. The sentence is a conditional of impossibility: 'if a man is able to count the dust of the earth, also your seed will be counted.' Rashi and Onkelos both take the meaning plainly: as the dust cannot be counted, neither can the seed. Radak calls it hyperbole, like 'the sand of the sea' and 'the stars of heaven' in Genesis 22:17, and records a midrash that dust is for the times they fail God (trampled) and stars for the times they serve him. The KJV 'so that if a man can number' is accurate, but its 'then shall thy seed also be numbered' tilts it toward a prediction, where the Hebrew is a negative by implication. Note the root repeated: mnh, 'count', appears twice, 'to count (limnot)' and 'will be counted (yimmaneh)', and the verb 'I will set' (samti) is the same used of placing a thing firmly. For a man who, at this moment, has no child, the words carry weight. The contrast with Lot, who took the visible well-watered plain, is complete: Abram is given what cannot be measured.

philological_notes.note: The root 'to count' is repeated: the man who tries to count the dust, and the seed that would be counted. The wordplay makes the impossibility logical: only if the first can be done can the second.
'Like the dust of the earth'. Radak calls this hyperbole in the manner of Genesis 22:17.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, walk about in the land, to its length and to its breadth, for to you I will give it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, Abram. Walk the land — its length, its breadth, every road of it — for I will give it to you.
verses.directors_commentary: Two imperatives, 'arise' and 'walk about', turn a vision into an action. The verb is in the reflexive stem (hithalekh), 'walk to and fro', the same form used of God walking in Eden and of Enoch and Noah walking with God, so the movement has a flavour of presence as well as travel. Radak assigns the directions: length is east to west, breadth is north to south. In the ancient world, walking a property's bounds was a recognised way of taking possession; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan makes this explicit by adding that he should 'make a claim of possession' (chezqata) in it. Ramban hesitates: it may be a mere permission, or a command to claim the gift, which he thinks Abram fulfilled when he went east to west to the Philistines. The actors should play it as a summons, not a tour. The KJV 'walk through the land' loses the back-and-forth of the reflexive, and its 'for I will give it unto thee' moves the 'to you' from the front of the clause, where the Hebrew puts it (lekha ettenennah), to the back. The ASV restores the order.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive imperative: to walk back and forth, to roam. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan glosses it as acquiring a legal claim by walking the land.
'To its length and to its breadth.' Radak makes length east–west and breadth north–south.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram tented, and came, and dwelt by the oaks of Mamre, which [are] in Hebron, and built there an altar to YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: So Abram struck his tents and moved on. He came at last to the great oaks of Mamre, at Hebron, and there he settled; and there, beneath the trees, he built an altar to the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: Three verbs in quick succession — he tented, he came, he dwelt — carry Abram out of the borderland and into the hill country. The first verb, vayye'ehal, is made from the noun 'tent' (ohel): literally, 'he tented', and the sense is that he pulled up and pitched again. Sforno hears two stages, moving his herds' tents here and there, then coming and settling at the oaks. The place is 'the oaks of Mamre', not the 'plain' of the KJV. That rendering follows the Aramaic of Onkelos (meshrei, 'plains'), but the Hebrew eilonei is 'great trees', oaks or terebinths, which in the ancient Near East were landmarks and sacred places. The KJV and Webster 'plain' therefore erases the tree. Rashi says Mamre is the name of a man, and Radak adds that the grove belonged to him, a different place from the oak of Moreh in Genesis 12:6. Hebron stands in the hills of Judah, about 30 km south of Jerusalem and nearly 1,000 m above sea level, a cooler, upland pasture, a contrast to the heat of the Jordan plain. Abram's response to a promise is, as before, an altar: where he settles, he builds, and Radak says he called on people there in the name of YHWH. The verse ends on the divine name, the same word as in 13:13: Sodom sins against YHWH, and Abram builds him an altar.

philological_notes.note: A denominative verb from 'tent' (ohel): 'he tented', that is, he pitched or moved his tent. Radak reads it as moving from place to place until he came to the oaks.

'The great trees of Mamre', oaks or terebinths (BDB). Onkelos translates 'plains of Mamre', which is the source of the KJV 'plain'. Radak says this is not the oak of Moreh from Genesis 12:6, and Rashi takes Mamre as a personal name.

events.title: Abram goes up from Egypt to Bethel
events.narrative_summary: Abram leaves Egypt with his wife, Lot and all he owns, very rich in livestock, silver and gold. He travels by stages from the Negeb to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had stood.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when Pharaoh sends Abram away (12:20). The text gives no duration. urim travel Egypt–Negeb–Bethel: ~555 km by road, 17 days for a laden donkey at 32 km a day. With flocks and herds I took about a month, margin one week. 'Journeys' (13:3) implies stages. The tier is REGNAL_YEAR as the scene falls under the age-75 frame of Gen 12.

events.title: Abram calls on the LORD at the first altar
events.narrative_summary: At the altar he had made earlier between Bethel and Ai, Abram calls on the name of the LORD.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the arrival at the place (13:3–4). Calling on the name takes hours, the exact time is unspecified, margin a day. REGNAL_YEAR because the text gives no time word of its own.

events.title: The herdsmen of Abram and Lot quarrel
events.narrative_summary: Lot also has flocks, herds and tents, and the land cannot support both men together. Their herdsmen quarrel while Canaanites and Perizzites live in the land.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no interval. I placed the strife about half a year after the altar (flocks growing), lasting about two months, margin six months. REGNAL_YEAR because the scene falls under the age frame of Gen 12 and no time word is given.

events.title: Abram proposes that he and Lot part
events.narrative_summary: Abram asks Lot to end the strife between them, since they are kin, and offers him the choice of any direction: if Lot goes left he will go right, and the reverse.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A speech after the strife (13:8), following continuously; a few minutes. The margin of a week allows for the time it took Abram to act after the strife began. REGNAL_YEAR: the speech has no time word (nor does the strife in 13:7) and falls under the chapter's year frame.

events.title: Lot chooses the Jordan valley and moves east
events.narrative_summary: Lot looks over the well-watered plain of the Jordan, like the garden of the LORD and like Egypt, before Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed. He chooses it, travels east, and the two men part.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Directly follows Abram's offer (13:10). Looking and choosing take hours; the move east starts in the same scene, so 3 hours, margin a day. REGNAL_YEAR: the scene follows the proposal directly but carries no time word of its own.

events.title: Lot settles in the cities of the plain near Sodom
events.narrative_summary: Abram stays in Canaan; Lot lives in the cities of the plain and pitches his tent toward Sodom, whose men are very wicked sinners before the LORD.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: urim travel Bethel–Sodom, donkey: 82 km straight, ~102 km by road, about 3 days at 32 km a day. Lot moves with flocks, herds and tents (13:5), as Abram did on his ascent from Egypt, so I took 4–6 days: offset 5 days after his departure, a week for the settling, margin one week. REGNAL_YEAR because the verse gives no time word.

events.title: The LORD promises Abram the whole land
events.narrative_summary: After Lot has left, the LORD tells Abram to look in all directions, promises him all the land he sees and descendants like the dust of the earth, and tells him to walk through the land.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'After Lot was separated from him' (13:14): the word comes after Lot's departure. I put it 2 days after Lot's departure ends the separation, margin one week. Rashi says the word was withheld while the wicked one was with Abram; Sforno gives a different reason. The tier is REGNAL_YEAR, as no day or hour is given.

events.title: Abram moves to Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar
events.narrative_summary: Abram moves his tent, comes to live by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron, and builds an altar to the LORD there.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Bethel–Hebron is about 58 km by road, 1.5 days by donkey (urim travel). The text gives no interval after the promise, so I set one week after it, duration 2 days for the move and altar, margin two weeks, REGNAL_YEAR.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Because the herdsmen quarrel (13:7), Abram asks Lot to part so there will be no strife between them (13:8).
The LORD speaks to Abram 'after Lot was separated from him' (13:14), so the separation made room for the promise, although the text does not say it caused it.
Abram offers Lot the choice of any direction (13:9), and Lot chooses the Jordan plain and goes (13:10–11).

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name: the Hebrew means 'shepherds of Abram's livestock'.
entities.summary_bio: The men who tend Abram's flocks and herds. Their quarrel with Lot's herdsmen over grazing and water in Genesis 13:7 leads to the separation of the two households.

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name: the Hebrew means 'shepherds of Lot's livestock'.
entities.summary_bio: The men who tend Lot's flocks, herds and tents. They quarrel with Abram's herdsmen, since the land cannot support both large households together.

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name: the Hebrew means 'men of Sodom'.
entities.summary_bio: The inhabitants of Sodom. The narrator tells us they are wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly, a note that darkens Lot's choice of the plain.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'villagers' or 'dwellers in open country', though the origin is debated.
entities.summary_bio: A people living in the land of Canaan alongside the Canaanites, mentioned in Genesis 13:7 to show that the land was already occupied while Abram and Lot quarrelled.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; sometimes explained as 'submersion' or 'tribute', but this is unproven.
entities.summary_bio: A city of the Jordan plain, paired with Sodom. The narrator names it as destined for destruction by the LORD.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'association' or 'league', from a root meaning 'to join'.
entities.summary_bio: A town in the hill country of Judah. The trees of Mamre, where Abram settles and builds an altar, are said to be at Hebron.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; sometimes linked to a root for 'burning' or 'scorching', but this is unproven.
entities.summary_bio: A city of the Jordan plain, near which Lot pitches his tent. Its people are described as exceedingly wicked and sinful before the LORD, and the narrator notes that the LORD would destroy it.

entities.etymology_meaning: 'Small' or 'insignificant', probably; the later story of Genesis 19 explains the name this way.
entities.summary_bio: A town at the edge of the Jordan plain, used in Genesis 13:10 to mark how far the well-watered plain extended toward the south.

components.label_value: Dwelling in the land of Canaan
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 13:12: 'Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan'.

components.label_value: Dwelling at the trees of Mamre
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 13:18: Abram moved his tent and dwelt at the oaks of Mamre at Hebron.

components.label_value: Offspring like the dust of the earth
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 13:16: the LORD will make Abram's seed like the dust of the earth.

components.label_value: Dwelling in the plain near Sodom
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 13:12: Lot dwelt in the cities of the plain and moved his tent as far as Sodom.
Gen 13:5 says Lot also had sheep, cattle and tents; 13:6 says their possessions were too great to dwell together.

components.label_value: Wicked and sinful before the LORD
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 13:13: the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram moves his tent to the trees of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar to the LORD there.
system_instances.significance_note: It claims the new dwelling place for worship, and sets Hebron as the patriarchs' centre in the land.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Back at the altar he had made earlier between Bethel and Ai, Abram calls on the name of the LORD.
system_instances.significance_note: It restores the worship begun in Genesis 12:8 after the Egyptian detour, and marks Bethel as Abram's return point.

system_instances.outcome_summary: After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to look in all four directions, promises him and his seed all the land he sees for ever, and promises seed like the dust of the earth.
system_instances.significance_note: It confirms and widens the promise of 12:7 at the moment Abram yields the best land, and the order to walk through the land marks it as his.

edges.description: Abram, citing their kinship, offers Lot first choice of the land so the two households can separate peacefully.
Lot, seeing the well-watered Jordan plain, chooses all of it for himself and journeys east.
The LORD tells Abram to arise and walk through the land in its length and breadth, since it will be given to him.
The LORD promises Abram and his seed all the land he sees, for ever.
